opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that "poem poem poem" example is a really instructive one, because I don't think anybody sitting in a room designing a test suite would have written that down as a test case. And that's sort of the point. It wasn't a sophisticated adversarial attack in the traditional sense. It was almost a degenerate input, and yet it caused the model to diverge from its normal behavior and start emitting what appeared to be memorized training data, some of which could contain personal information. So from a privacy standpoint, it's exactly the kind of thing you worry about.

The way I think about it is that we're dealing with systems whose input space is essentially unbounded. Any string of text is a legitimate input. In classical software testing you might hope to cover the important branches of the code, but here the "code" is billions of parameters and the behavior is emergent. There's no specification you can test against exhaustively. So I'm somewhat skeptical of the idea that you can just enumerate a list of bad behaviors and check them off.

That said, I don't think the answer is to throw up our hands. A few things matter. One is that red-teaming has to be broad and somewhat creative, and it helps to bring in people with very different backgrounds and intuitions, not just ML engineers, because the failure modes are often surprising. Another is that you want more principled guarantees where you can get them. On the privacy side, for example, differential privacy gives you a provable bound on how much any individual's data can influence the model, regardless of what clever prompt somebody comes up with later. That's a fundamentally different kind of assurance than "we tested a lot of prompts and didn't find a leak." It's a guarantee that holds against all possible queries, including ones nobody has thought of yet.

The tradeoff, of course, is that those guarantees come at some cost in accuracy or utility, and at the scale of these models it's still an active research question how to make that tradeoff palatable. But I think the general lesson from examples like the "poem" attack is that empirical testing alone will always be playing catch-up. You find one hole, you patch it, and someone finds another. So ideally you want a combination: aggressive, diverse empirical probing on one hand, and wherever possible, design-time constraints with actual mathematical guarantees on the other. And I'd add that we should be humble about the fact that we're deploying these systems while our understanding of their behavior is still pretty incomplete.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the "poem" example is actually a really nice illustration of something that's deeply different about these systems compared to the kinds of models we had in machine learning even five or ten years ago. For context, what happened there was that if you asked one of these chat models to repeat a single word over and over forever, it would do that for a while, and then at some point it would sort of drift off and start emitting what turned out to be verbatim chunks of its training data, including in some cases things like people's contact information. And nobody designed that behavior, nobody anticipated it, and I think it's fair to say that even in hindsight nobody can give you a clean mechanistic explanation of why it happens.

So the way I think about testing is that we have to be honest about what kind of object we're dealing with. These are enormously high-dimensional, essentially unstructured functions, and the input space is all of natural language. That's not a space you can enumerate. When I worked on things like learning theory, or even on fairness and privacy in more traditional models, you at least had a well-defined input domain and a well-defined notion of what the model was supposed to compute, and you could reason about generalization or about worst-case behavior with some mathematical precision. Here, the specification itself is fuzzy. "Don't do anything weird" is not a formal property.

So I think testing has to be adversarial and it has to be ongoing. The analogy I keep coming back to is computer security rather than classical software testing. You don't prove that a system is secure; you red-team it, you have people whose job it is to try to break it, and you accept that the attack surface is open-ended. The "poem" thing was found by researchers essentially poking at the model in ways its designers hadn't thought about, and that's going to be the pattern. Every time you patch one of these, you've closed one hole in a space that has an unbounded number of them.

Now, that's not purely pessimistic. There's a lot you can do on the structured side. If what you care about is memorization and privacy leakage, there are principled tools, things like differential privacy in training, which give you actual guarantees rather than just the absence of a known exploit. If what you care about is a specific class of harmful outputs, you can build targeted evaluations and automate them at scale, and you can use other models to generate adversarial inputs rather than relying on humans alone. So I'd say the mature approach is to combine the two: use formal methods and training-time interventions where you can actually state the property you want, and use large-scale adversarial testing for everything else, with the understanding that the second category is always going to be incomplete.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that we'll eventually arrive at a test suite you run once and then declare the model safe. I don't think that's the nature of these systems. It's more like you're maintaining a relationship with the model over time, continuously probing it, and treating every surprise as information about how little we still understand about what's going on inside.

r001.rationale: The response says natural-language inputs cannot be exhaustively enumerated, but does not state that exhaustive testability would imply a substantially less powerful model.

r002.rationale: The response describes ongoing adversarial testing and patching, but does not say that a working hack can stop working within a week.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a good example of how difficult it is to know what you’ve ruled out when you test one of these models. You can ask it a lot of questions, you can have people deliberately try to make it misbehave, and that’s valuable. But asking it to repeat “poem” indefinitely is a rather unusual thing to do. It’s not obvious that a conventional test suite would include that.

There’s an important distinction between testing behavior on inputs that resemble ordinary use and testing against somebody who is actively searching for a failure. In the second case, the person can adapt. They can try something, look at the response, and use that information to choose the next thing they try. That’s a much harder problem than measuring average performance on a fixed collection of prompts.

So I’d view this kind of testing as an ongoing adversarial process. When somebody finds a failure, you want to understand whether it’s an isolated example or a symptom of something broader. Fixing that particular prompt is useful, but it doesn’t establish that a slightly different prompt won’t produce the same behavior. The challenge is moving from a growing list of examples to a more systematic understanding of when and why these failures occur.

r001.rationale: The response says exhaustive testing is difficult and that conventional test suites may miss unusual inputs, but it does not state that being able to test every possible input would imply the model is substantially less powerful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of that as an example of why testing these models is so challenging. You can evaluate a model on a large collection of questions and find that it behaves quite well, and then somebody tries something that seems almost nonsensical—like asking it to repeat “poem” indefinitely—and discovers behavior you weren’t anticipating.

The question is how to turn that kind of discovery into a systematic testing methodology. What class of failures does it represent? Can we find related failures? And if we fix this particular example, have we addressed the underlying problem, or just made that particular prompt stop working?

That’s where adversarial testing is valuable. You want people actively looking for ways to make the system misbehave, including ways its designers wouldn’t think to try. But passing those tests is evidence about the tests you ran; it isn’t a guarantee about everything someone might ask the model tomorrow.
